clinicalPearls: One of the commonest congenital urinary tract anomalies, ranging from a partial (incomplete) duplication where the two ureters join before the bladder, to complete duplication with two separate ureteric orifices

The Weigert-Meyer rule governs complete duplication: the upper-pole ureter inserts more caudally and medially (ectopic, prone to obstruction and ureterocele), while the lower-pole ureter inserts more superolaterally and is prone to vesicoureteric reflux
Many duplex systems are incidental and asymptomatic and require no treatment

Symptomatic presentations include urinary tract infection, antenatal hydronephrosis, obstruction of the upper moiety, reflux into the lower moiety, and continuous incontinence in girls from an ectopic ureter inserting below the sphincter
In partial duplication, ureteroureteral (yo-yo) reflux between the two limbs can cause stasis and infection
Imaging aims to define which moiety is affected, its function, and the presence of reflux, obstruction, or an ectopic insertion/ureterocele
Management is dictated by function and pathology, from surveillance to upper-pole heminephrectomy, ureteric reimplantation, or ureteroureterostomy
reference.pathophysiology: A duplex collecting system arises when the ureteric bud undergoes abnormal branching during development. Early splitting of a single bud produces incomplete duplication with a bifid system joining before the bladder, whereas two separate ureteric buds produce complete duplication with two ureters and orifices. The differing sites at which the buds contact the developing bladder explain the Weigert-Meyer relationship: the more caudally arising upper-pole ureter inserts ectopically and inferomedially, predisposing to obstruction and ureterocele, while the lower-pole ureter inserts superolaterally with a short intramural tunnel, predisposing to reflux. The associated renal moieties may show variable dysplasia depending on the position of bud contact with the metanephric blastema.
additionalDifferentials: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction of a single system
Ureterocele or ectopic ureter in a single system
Continuous incontinence from other cause in girls
additionalInvestigations: Renal and bladder ultrasound to demonstrate duplication and moiety dilatation
Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) to detect reflux, usually into the lower moiety
MAG3 or DMSA renography to assess function of each moiety and drainage
MR urography to define complex ductal anatomy and ectopic insertions
Cystoscopy to locate ureteric orifices and any ureterocele
redFlags: Obstruction of the upper moiety with declining function or infection
High-grade reflux into the lower moiety with recurrent pyelonephritis or scarring
Continuous urinary leakage from an ectopic ureter indicating an insertion below the sphincter
Urosepsis in an obstructed or refluxing duplex system
reference.prognosis: Asymptomatic duplex systems have an excellent prognosis and need no intervention; symptomatic systems generally do well when the specific pathology (obstruction, reflux, or ectopia) is appropriately treated, with overall renal function usually preserved.
pitfalls: Misapplying the Weigert-Meyer rule and treating the wrong moiety
Missing an ectopic ureter as the cause of continuous incontinence in a girl
Overlooking a poorly functioning obstructed upper pole on standard imaging
Assuming all duplex systems require surgery when many are incidental
management: Observe incidental, asymptomatic duplex systems, which require no intervention
Prevent and treat urinary tract infection promptly, using antibiotic prophylaxis where there is significant vesicoureteric reflux or recurrent infection
Decompress an obstructing ureterocele endoscopically by incision or puncture
Offer reconstructive surgery for symptomatic disease: upper-pole heminephrectomy for a non-functioning obstructed moiety, ureteric reimplantation for troublesome reflux, or ureteroureterostomy
Assess and monitor moiety function and drainage with MAG3 or DMSA renography, and surveil for reflux nephropathy and scarring
Manage jointly through urology and paediatric nephrology, tailoring treatment to the affected moiety and its pathology
